Precalculus | Quarter 2 | Unit 4: Trigonometry

The Jump-Range Identity

Why 45° goes furthest

Duration
55 minutes
Grade level
Grades 11–12
Topic
Trigonometric Identities
Standards
HSF-TF.C.8, HSF-TF.C.9, HSA-SSE.A.2

Students prove and use the Pythagorean identities, the sum and difference formulas and the double-angle formulas, and use sin 2θ = 2sinθcosθ to explain why a 45° takeoff maximises a jump’s range on level ground.

2Learning objectives

By the end of this lesson, students will be able to:

  • Use sin2θ + cos2θ = 1 and its related forms.
  • Use the sum and difference formulas to find exact values.
  • Use double-angle formulas.
  • Verify identities and apply them to the projectile range formula.

3Essential question

How can rewriting a trig expression reveal the best launch angle for a jump?

5MTB connection

The double-angle identity turns the jump-range formula into a single sine, which shows at a glance that 45° gives the longest jump on level ground, and that 30° and 60° go equally far (but 60° goes much higher).

The identity 1 + tan2θ = sec2θ is the trail-length fact from Lesson 4.4 in disguise: surface length = run × secθ = run × √1 + grade2.

The mathOn the trail
sin 2θHow the range depends on angle
Maximum of sin 2θBest takeoff angle (45°)
sin(180° − x) = sin xTwo angles, same range
1 + tan2θ = sec2θSurface length from grade

The Range Investigation
